documents.dateNote: Date at the head of the letter; the FSB published it on 31 August 2026 (press release page). The letter carries no disclaimer.

records.statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 on artificial intelligence and machine learning in financial services states that if many market participants use similar AI and machine-learning programmes, the resulting correlated risks may entail financial stability risks and, as with any herding behaviour, could amplify financial shocks.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The report states that there was no evidence of this occurring at the time and frames it as a possibility with greater adoption; its analysis is described as preliminary.

evidence.passage: if many market participants come to use similar AI and machine learning programmes in areas such as credit scoring or financial market activities, the consequent correlated risks may entail financial stability risks.

While there is no evidence of this occurring to date, this could become relevant with greater adoption of such trading strategies. As with any herding behaviour in the market, this has the potential to amplify financial shocks.

evidence.locator: Section 5.3 "Networks and interconnectedness", PDF p. 35 (printed p. 31)
evidence.passage: If a critical segment of financial institutions rely on the same data sources and algorithmic strategies, then under certain market conditions a shock to those data sources … could affect that segment as if it were a single node.

records.statement: The FSB report of 27 June 2017 on financial stability implications from FinTech states that social trading and robo-advice could show greater herding behaviour than traditional portfolio allocation if risk models are highly correlated through reliance on similar algorithms, and notes that it found no empirical evidence so far of convergence of robo-advisors’ algorithms or portfolios.
records.missing: The passage does not name AI or machine-learning models; it concerns robo-advice and social trading algorithms generally.
records.qualification: The passage concerns robo-advice and social trading algorithms; it does not name AI or machine learning (the report’s glossary says robo-advisors "can also include machine learning"). Recorded as context to the November 2017 articulation.

evidence.locator: Section 3 (financial stability risks), PDF p. 24 (printed p. 20)
evidence.passage: Social trading and robo-advice could potentially exhibit greater herding behaviour than traditional portfolio allocation methods – for example, if risk models are highly correlated due to reliance on similar algorithms – thereby potentially increasing the amplitude of swings in asset prices.
we found no empirical evidence so far on convergence of robo-advisors’ algorithms or portfolios.

records.statement: In the IMF Departmental Paper of 22 October 2021, IMF staff authors El Bachir Boukherouaa, Khaled AlAjmi, Jose Deodoro, Aquiles Farias and Rangachary Ravikumar write that concentration of third-party AI/ML algorithm providers could drive greater homogeneity in risk assessments and credit decisions, with a risk of uniformity (herding), and that widespread AI/ML use could increase procyclicality.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. A staff paper attributed to its authors.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3, section F "Impact on Financial Stability", second bullet (HTML)
evidence.passage: The concentration of third-party AI/ML algorithm providers could drive greater homogeneity in risk assessments and credit decisions in the financial sector, which, coupled with rising interconnectedness, could create the conditions for a buildup of systemic risks.
The widespread use of AI/ML could potentially increase procyclicality of financial conditions.

records.statement: Chapter 3 of the IMF Global Financial Stability Report of October 2024, prepared by IMF staff of the Monetary and Capital Markets Department, states that AI models may herd and produce similar decisions, especially in stress periods, resulting in procyclical financial stability risks.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The chapter also states that AI use in capital markets is still relatively nascent and that its financial stability risks currently appear contained.

evidence.locator: Section "Summarizing the Financial Stability Challenges: Current and Prospective", "Increased market speed and volatility under stress" (HTML)
evidence.passage: AI models may herd and produce rather similar decisions, especially during stress periods resulting in procyclical financial stability risks.
The use of AI in capital markets is still relatively nascent, and currently the financial stability risks associated with its adoption appear contained.

records.statement: The FSB report of 14 November 2024 on the financial stability implications of artificial intelligence states that widespread use of common AI models and data sources could increase correlations in trading, lending and pricing, amplifying market stress, and sets out herding, network externalities, limited choice and lack of transparency as drivers.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The report states that if financial institutions mainly use LLMs for internal efficiencies, the impact on market correlations is likely to be minimal.

evidence.locator: Executive summary, "Market correlations", PDF p. 5 (printed p. 1)
evidence.passage: The widespread use of common AI models and data sources could lead to increased correlations in trading, lending, and pricing. This could amplify market stress, exacerbate liquidity crunches, and increase asset price vulnerabilities.
if FIs primarily use LLMs for internal efficiencies, such as document drafting, employee education and information retrieval, the impact on market correlations is likely to be minimal.

records.statement: In ESRB Advisory Scientific Committee Report No 16 of December 2025, Stephen Cecchetti, Robin L. Lumsdaine, Tuomas Peltonen and Antonio Sánchez Serrano write that widespread use of similar AI models can lead to correlated exposures and amplified market reactions, listing model uniformity among AI features that can exacerbate systemic risk.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. An Advisory Scientific Committee report attributed to its authors; the ESRB states it is not its official stance. A footnote states that the executive summary is an edited version of a draft produced by an AI tool.

evidence.passage: Model uniformity: Widespread use of similar AI models can lead to correlated exposures and amplified market reactions.
If many institutions rely on the same AI model or data source, a flaw in that model or a corrupt data update could lead to simultaneous failure

records.statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 states that AI and machine-learning services are increasingly offered by a few large technology firms, that third-party dependencies could give rise to new systemically important players, and that these dependencies could have systemic effects if such a firm faced a major disruption or insolvency.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The report frames these as possible future developments ("may in the future").

evidence.passage: the emergence of a relatively small number of advanced third-party providers in AI and machine learning could increase concentration of some functions in the financial system.
AI and machine learning services are increasingly being offered by a few large technology firms.
These third-party dependencies and interconnections could have systemic effects if such a large firm were to face a major disruption or insolvency.

records.statement: In the IMF Departmental Paper of 22 October 2021, Boukherouaa, AlAjmi, Deodoro, Farias and Ravikumar write that AI/ML service providers could become systemically important participants in financial market infrastructure, increasing vulnerability to single points of failure.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. A staff paper attributed to its authors.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3, section F "Impact on Financial Stability", first bullet (HTML)
evidence.passage: AI/ML service providers could become systemically important participants in financial market infrastructure due to the high specialization of AI/ML systems and network effects, which could increase the financial system’s vulnerability to single points of failure.

records.statement: In a speech of 11 July 2024 at the IMF/World Bank Constituency meeting in Moldova, Klaas Knot, Chair of the Financial Stability Board, said that concentration risk and third-party risks were among the most important AI risks identified, and that the market for generative AI models appears to rest on a handful of models.
records.qualification: The speaker’s view in his role as FSB Chair, not the FSB’s position (disclaimer recorded). He described the FSB’s update of its 2017 report as not yet concluded.

evidence.locator: Speech text, paragraph beginning "This year, we are updating"
evidence.passage: The most important ones are concentration risk, third-party risks, possible increases in herding behaviour, and model risk, including challenges with regard to explainability.

evidence.locator: Speech text, paragraph beginning "Many of the potential risks"
evidence.passage: Although there are lots of applications out there, in practice they all seem to be based on only a handful of models, perhaps just three or four.

records.statement: Chapter 3 of the IMF Global Financial Stability Report of October 2024, prepared by IMF staff, states that AI models and related IT services reside with a handful of key providers and that, if capital markets become too reliant on them, the failure of these providers may lead to market stress akin to the failure of key financial market utilities.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The chapter also reports that participants in the IMF outreach cited vendor concentration as a potential source of systemic risk (a relay of outreach views, given as context).

evidence.locator: Section "Summarizing the Financial Stability Challenges", "Increased operational risks as a result of reliance on a few key third-party AI service providers" (HTML)
evidence.passage: AI models and related information technology services currently reside with a handful of key providers with dominant computational power and established large language models.

If capital markets activities become too reliant on these models, the failure of these providers may lead to market stress akin to the failure of key financial market utilities such as clearing houses.

records.statement: The FSB report of 14 November 2024 states that reliance on specialised hardware, cloud services and pre-trained models has increased AI-related third-party dependencies and that the highly concentrated market for these products could expose financial institutions to operational vulnerabilities and systemic risk.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.locator: Executive summary, "Third-party dependencies and service provider concentration", PDF p. 5 (printed p. 1)
evidence.passage: The market for these products and services is also highly concentrated, which could expose FIs to operational vulnerabilities and systemic risk from disruptions affecting key service providers.

records.statement: In his letter of 28 August 2026 to G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors, Andrew Bailey, Chair of the Financial Stability Board, wrote that frontier AI could alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber risk in a way that could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially because of highly concentrated third-party service providers.
records.missing: The concentrated third-party service providers are not stated to be providers of AI models, data or computing; the concentration is named as an amplifier of cyber risk from frontier AI.
records.qualification: The Chair’s letter, attributed to him; it is not stated to be an FSB decision. The concentration passage is tied to cyber risk from frontier AI.

evidence.passage: which could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially due to highly concentrated third-party service providers.

records.statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 states that predictable patterns in the behaviour of automated trading strategies could be used by insiders or cybercriminals to manipulate market prices, and that uses of AI and machine learning should be assessed for risks including cybersecurity.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The manipulation passage concerns automated trading strategies, in a section on AI and machine learning in markets.

evidence.passage: advanced optimisation techniques and predictable patterns in the behaviour of automated trading strategies could be used by insiders or by cybercriminals to manipulate market prices.
It will be important to assess uses of AI and machine learning in view of their risks, including adherence to relevant protocols on data privacy, conduct risks, and cybersecurity.

records.statement: In the IMF Departmental Paper of 22 October 2021, Boukherouaa, AlAjmi, Deodoro, Farias and Ravikumar write that AI/ML adoption increases the scope for cyber threats and brings new cyber risks, and that the cybersecurity regulatory perimeter could be expanded to cover AI/ML-specific threats.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. A staff paper attributed to its authors.

evidence.passage: AI/ML adoption increases the scope for cyber threats and brings in new unique cyber risks.
The regulatory perimeter of cybersecurity requirements in the financial sector could be expanded to cover AI/ML-specific cyber threats.

records.statement: In IMF FinTech Note 2023/006 of 22 August 2023, Ghiath Shabsigh and El Bachir Boukherouaa write that generative AI could be exploited for more sophisticated phishing and impersonation, which could increase identity theft or fraud, and that deepfakes could inflict serious damage on organisations and individuals.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. A staff note attributed to its authors.

evidence.passage: This emerging technology could be exploited to generate more sophisticated phishing messages and emails or to present opportunities for malicious actors to impersonate individuals or organizations, leading to increased identity theft or fraud.
The proliferation of deepfakes, resulting in more realistic videos, audios, or images, could inflict serious damage on both organizations and individuals.

records.statement: The FSB report of 14 November 2024 states that AI uptake by malicious actors could increase the frequency and impact of cyber attacks and that generative AI could increase financial fraud and the spread of disinformation in financial markets.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.passage: AI uptake by malicious actors could increase the frequency and impact of cyber attacks.
GenAI could increase financial fraud and the ability of malicious actors to generate and spread disinformation in financial markets.

records.statement: Chapter 3 of the IMF Global Financial Stability Report of October 2024, prepared by IMF staff, states that fraud, disinformation and deepfakes will likely become more sophisticated as AI advances and could be used to manipulate financial markets and asset prices.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.locator: Section "Summarizing the Financial Stability Challenges", "Increased market manipulation and cyber risks" (HTML)
evidence.passage: Fraud, disinformation, and deepfakes will likely become more sophisticated as AI advances and could be used by bad actors to manipulate financial markets and asset prices.

records.statement: In his letter of 28 August 2026 to G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors, Andrew Bailey, Chair of the Financial Stability Board, wrote that for the financial system the most immediate concern about frontier AI models is their potential impact on cyber risk.
records.qualification: The Chair’s letter, attributed to him; it is not stated to be an FSB decision.

evidence.passage: For the financial system, the most immediate concern is the potential impact of frontier AI on cyber risk. Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber risk

records.statement: The FSB report of 27 June 2017 on financial stability implications from FinTech states, in its case study on AI and machine learning, that key risks include the opacity and lack of auditability of "black box" algorithms, and that the auditability of AI models used by banks might be difficult to achieve given model validation practices that require models to be explained to regulators.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The annex describes its findings as preliminary.

evidence.locator: Annex G "Case study on AI and machine learning", "Potential to undermine financial stability", PDF p. 60 (printed p. 56)
evidence.passage: Key risks include the opacity and lack of auditability of algorithms (in case of “black boxes”) and undesired changes to market structure.
Specifically, the “auditability” of the models might be difficult to achieve and not ensured in all cases.

records.statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 states that the lack of interpretability or auditability of AI and machine-learning methods could become a macro-level risk if not appropriately supervised, and that widespread use of opaque models would make it very difficult for firms and supervisors to predict how model-directed actions affect markets.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.passage: The lack of interpretability or ‘auditability’ of AI and machine learning methods has the potential to contribute to macro-level risk if not appropriately supervised by microprudential supervisors.
it would be very difficult for both firms and supervisors to predict how actions directed by models will affect markets.

records.statement: The EBA Report on Big Data and Advanced Analytics of January 2020 states that machine-learning models can become "black boxes" whose reasoning is hard to understand and verify, and that lack of explainability could be an important risk for models bought from third parties, which the acquiring institution must be able to validate.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The passage concerns explainability as an element of trustworthy use by institutions.

evidence.passage: ML models can quickly become “black boxes”, opaque systems for which the internal behaviour cannot be easily understood, and for which therefore it is not easy to understand (and verify) how a model has reached a certain conclusion or prediction.
Lack of explainability could represent an important risk in the case of AI/ML models developed by external third parties and then sold as opaque black box packages.

records.statement: The EBA follow-up report of August 2023 on machine learning for IRB models states that the main challenge discussed for using machine-learning techniques in IRB models is their complexity, which leads to difficulties in explaining their results, traceability and adequate understanding by management functions.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The scope is internal ratings-based credit risk models of banks.

evidence.passage: The DP discussed as the main pivotal challenge for using ML techniques the complexity, which leads, to challenges in explaining their results. This goes hand in hand with the problem of traceability and ensuring an adequate understanding by the management functions.

records.statement: The FSB report of 14 November 2024 states that the complexity and limited explainability of some AI methods, and the difficulty of assessing data quality for widely used models, could increase model risk for financial institutions lacking robust AI governance.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.locator: Executive summary, "Model risk, data quality and governance", PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 1–2)
evidence.passage: The complexity and limited explainability of some AI methods and the difficulty of assessing data quality for widely used AI models … could increase model risk for FIs that lack robust AI governance.
evidence.note: The ellipsis marks the page break between PDF pp. 5 and 6 and the printed page number there; no words of the sentence are omitted (cross-family check, A2.25).

crossFamily.result: corrected: the evidence note says the ellipsis omits no words. Classification agreed.

records.statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 states, in its section on uses by central banks and prudential authorities, that natural language processing tools may help authorities detect, measure, predict and anticipate market volatility, liquidity risks, financial stress, housing prices and unemployment.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The report cites studies and a Banca d’Italia study described as in progress.

evidence.locator: Section 3.4.3 "SupTech: uses and potential uses by central banks and prudential authorities", PDF p. 25 (printed p. 21)
evidence.passage: Machine learning can be applied to systemic risk identification and risk propagation channels. Specifically, NLP tools may help authorities to detect, measure, predict, and anticipate, among other things, market volatility, liquidity risks, financial stress, housing prices, and unemployment.

crossFamily.result: earliest located institutional text for U05 (derived) for now; an earlier institutional text, agreed, is to be drafted (C32).
crossFamily.headline: Second check (C32): the checker read the Bank of England’s One Bank Research Agenda discussion paper (February 2015; launched 25 February 2015) in a March 2015 capture of the official address (web.archive.org; the official addresses now return 404) and finds that its Theme 4 (printed pp. 23–24, PDF pp. 24–25) meets U05 in the Bank’s voice: machine-learning analysis of textual information, including central-bank communications. Agreed. The record is to be drafted from the archived copy before admission part 2; this environment could not reach web.archive.org on 2026-11-04 (connection closed by the proxy). It would replace this report as the earliest located institutional text for U05; it does not displace ECB Working Paper 352 (April 2004).

records.statement: In the IMF Departmental Paper of 22 October 2021, Boukherouaa, AlAjmi, Deodoro, Farias and Ravikumar write that AI/ML systems could help central banks improve their understanding of economic and financial developments and support better-tuned monetary and macroprudential policies, and that central bank experiments have focused on near-term forecasting and market sentiment.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The authors add that the use of AI/ML for policymaking should remain subject to good judgment.

evidence.passage: AI/ML systems could help central banks improve their understanding of economic and financial developments, support better-tuned monetary and macroprudential policies, and improve central banks’ operations.
Experiments and research by central banks have focused on improving the near-term forecasting capacity and the monitoring of market sentiment to inform policy decisions.

records.statement: The FSB report of 27 June 2017 on financial stability implications from FinTech states, in its case study on AI and machine learning, that key potential benefits include applications of AI and machine learning in supervision, and that AI and machine learning can aid supervision by identifying new relationships in data.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The annex describes its findings as preliminary.

evidence.locator: Annex G, "Potential to support financial stability", PDF p. 60 (printed p. 56)
evidence.passage: Key potential benefits include various applications of AI and machine learning in supervision, internal audit and regulatory reporting, as well as the ability to better monitor risks.
AI and machine learning can aid supervision by allowing the identification of new relationships in data, without the filter of pre-specified models.
There is also a close link with “SupTech,” or the use of FinTech by supervisory authorities.
evidence.note: A glossary definition that does not mention AI; recorded only for the earliest located use of the name (audit, 2026-11-02).

records.statement: In ESRB Advisory Scientific Committee Report No 16 of December 2025, Cecchetti, Lumsdaine, Peltonen and Sánchez Serrano write that AI does not necessitate a full overhaul of the regulatory system but that it is almost surely necessary to consider significant reforms, and that risks from AI provider concentration, model uniformity and cyber-attacks may require fundamental changes beyond the current prudential framework.

engagement.rationale: Disputes the premise that the current prudential framework suffices, stating that specific AI risks may require fundamental changes beyond it.

records.qualification: An Advisory Scientific Committee report attributed to its authors, not the ESRB’s stance. evidence.passage: While, in general, we believe that the advent of AI does not necessitate a full overhaul of the existing regulatory system, it is almost surely necessary to consider significant reforms.
